x-m-m1-01.title: Finding a number with 12 divisors
x-m-m1-01.goal: Discover how divisors are built from the prime-factorized form, then find several numbers that fit the condition and check them.
x-m-m1-01.material:
A number N was prime factorized, and its only prime factors were 2 and 3. So N is the product of '2 multiplied a times' and '3 multiplied b times' (a and b are natural numbers that are at least 1).
For example, 12 = 2²×3 (2 multiplied twice, 3 multiplied once). If we write the divisors of 12 (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) as 'how many times 2 is multiplied, how many times 3 is multiplied,' we get the following.
Divisor 1: 2 zero times, 3 zero times / Divisor 2: 1 time, 0 times / Divisor 4: 2 times, 0 times / Divisor 3: 0 times, 1 time / Divisor 6: 1 time, 1 time / Divisor 12: 2 times, 1 time
x-m-m1-01.prereq.0: The meaning of divisors of a natural number
x-m-m1-01.prereq.1: Reading a prime-factorized form like 2²×3 (2² means 2 multiplied twice)
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.prompt: Which statement best explains why 12 has 6 divisors in the table above?
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.hint.0: In the table, write each divisor as a pair of the two counts, and see whether any pairs repeat.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many values the count can take for each prime factor.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.o.a: The larger of the count of 2s (2) and the count of 3s (1), plus 1
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the larger one and missed the divisors made by the other prime factor. Check in the table whether the choices for the two prime factors happen together.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.o.b: The count of 2s (2) times the count of 3s (1)
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.r.b: You multiplied the counts, but the result does not match the 6 divisors in the table. Check whether you counted the cases where the count is 0.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.o.c: The number of ways to pair one of the counts 0, 1, 2 for 2 with one of the counts 0, 1 for 3
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.r.c: You read each divisor in the table as a 'pair of two counts' and found the structure.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.o.d: The count of 2s (2) plus the count of 3s (1), plus the divisors 1 and 12
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.r.d: 1 and 12 are already in the table. Check whether you counted something twice.
x-m-m1-01.s.s1.explain: Each divisor in the table is made by choosing how many times 2 is multiplied (3 choices: 0, 1, 2) and how many times 3 is multiplied (2 choices: 0, 1). The two choices do not affect each other, so there are 3×2=6 divisors.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different numbers N that have exactly 12 divisors. Enter the two counts that make up N: a (how many times 2 is multiplied) and b (how many times 3 is multiplied).
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.hint.0: If a=1 and b=1, then N=6. Count the divisors of 6 and check whether they match the rule you just saw.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.hint.1: Change a and b, count how many choices each prime factor has for its count, and adjust them so that the relationship between those numbers of choices gives 12.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.var.a: a, the number of times 2 is multiplied
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.var.b: b, the number of times 3 is multiplied
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.fail.c2: This N does not have 12 divisors.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.explain: Examples: (a=3, b=2) gives N=72, which has 4×3=12 divisors; (5, 1) gives N=96; (2, 3) gives N=108; (1, 5) gives N=486. (3, 2) and (2, 3) give different numbers.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the N you found and write how you checked that it really has 12 divisors.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: There are two ways to check: listing the divisors yourself, or counting with the rule. Choose one.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Calculate the numbers you used for checking one more time.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is your checking method written with specific numbers?
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Could you use the method you wrote for other values of N in the same way?
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.model.0: 72=2³×3², so the count of 2s can be 4 choices (0, 1, 2, 3) and the count of 3s can be 3 choices (0, 1, 2). Pairing them and multiplying gives 4×3=12 divisors.
x-m-m1-01.s.s2.because.model.1: I listed the divisors of 72 myself: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. There were 12.

x-m-m1-02.title: Finding the wrong line in a greatest common divisor solution
x-m-m1-02.goal: Find the line where an error occurred in a solution that finds the greatest common divisor by prime factorization, then explain how to confirm the result is impossible and give the correct value.
x-m-m1-02.material: Minseo found the greatest common divisor of 36 and 60 by prime factorization and wrote the solution below. (2² means 2 squared, and 3² means 3 squared.)
x-m-m1-02.thinking.0: Finding where the error is in the solution
x-m-m1-02.thinking.1: Checking whether the result makes sense
x-m-m1-02.prereq.1: The meaning of common divisors and the greatest common divisor
x-m-m1-02.s.s1.line.1: The prime factors in both numbers are 2 and 3.
x-m-m1-02.s.s1.line.2: For each common prime factor, we take the one with the larger exponent. For 2 it is 2², and for 3 it is 3².
x-m-m1-02.s.s1.line.3: So the greatest common divisor is 2² × 3² = 36.
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.prompt: Write one way to confirm that 36 cannot be the greatest common divisor, and write the correct greatest common divisor.
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.hint.0: See whether either of the two numbers is not divisible by 36.
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether your corrected value divides both 36 and 60.
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the checking method you wrote really show that 36 is wrong?
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether 12 divides both 36 and 60?
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.model.0: 60 is not divisible by 36, so 36 cannot be a common divisor. Taking the smaller exponents gives 2²×3=12, which is correct.
x-m-m1-02.s.s2.model.1: 36 is not a divisor of 60. We have to choose the smaller exponent of each common prime factor, so it becomes 2²×3=12.

x-m-m1-03.title: Testing the claim 'a smaller number also has a smaller absolute value'
x-m-m1-03.goal: Build a counterexample to a generalization about absolute values and order of size, and find the condition under which it holds.
x-m-m1-03.material: Seoyun said, "Of two numbers, the smaller one also has the smaller absolute value. 3<7, and |3|=3 and |7|=7, so 3<7, right?" (|a| is read 'the absolute value of a,' and it is the distance between 0 and a on the number line.)
x-m-m1-03.thinking.0: Making a counterexample to the claim
x-m-m1-03.thinking.2: Finding the condition for it to hold
x-m-m1-03.prereq.0: Positions of integers and rational numbers on the number line
x-m-m1-03.prereq.1: The meaning of absolute value (distance from 0)
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.prompt: Make examples that go against Seoyun's claim using two numbers (a, b) where a<b but |a| is greater than |b|. You need two examples in which the sign of b is different (positive, 0, negative), such as one where b is positive and one where b is negative.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.hint.0: First test what happens when a is greater than 0.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which side of 0 a must be on the number line, then choose b.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.fail.c1: a is not less than b.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.ok.c2: The absolute value of a is greater than the absolute value of b.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.fail.c2: The absolute value of a is not greater than the absolute value of b.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.explain: a must be negative. Examples: (−5, 2) has −5<2 but |−5|=5>|2|=2, and (−5, −2) has −5<−2 but 5>2. Examples with b positive and with b negative are both possible.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.prompt: Choose one example you found and explain why Seoyun's claim is wrong.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.hint.0: Write the two numbers in your chosen example and their two absolute values side by side.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.hint.1: Think about how many examples it takes to break the word 'always.'
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: In your chosen example, does a<b really hold?
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show that the sizes of the absolute values come out opposite to Seoyun's claim?
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.model.0: For example, −5<2, but the absolute value of −5, which is 5, is greater than the absolute value of 2, which is 2, so the claim is wrong. Even one counterexample makes 'always' false.
x-m-m1-03.s.s1.because.model.1: −3<−1, but |−3|=3 and |−1|=1, so the absolute value is not smaller. Because of this case, the claim does not hold.
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.prompt: When can we say that 'if a<b, then |a|<|b|' must hold?
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one number that fits the condition of each choice, and check whether the counterexample you made earlier could appear under that condition.
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.hint.1: If a counterexample can appear under the condition, it does not fit 'must hold.'
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.r.a: For negative numbers, the order is actually reversed. −5<−2, but the absolute values are 5>2.
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.o.b: When both numbers are at least 0
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.r.b: You saw that for numbers that are at least 0, the absolute value is the number itself, so the order of size carries over unchanged.
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.o.c: When the larger number b is positive
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.r.c: Even if b is positive, it breaks if a is a negative number farther from 0 than b is (−5<2).
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.o.d: When the smaller number a is negative
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.r.d: If a is negative, the claim sometimes holds, as in −2<5, and sometimes breaks, as in −5<2, so it is not 'must hold.'
x-m-m1-03.s.s2.explain: If both numbers are at least 0, the absolute value is the number itself, so the order is the same. If a is negative, the claim holds by chance in some cases like −2<5, but it breaks in cases like −5<2, so we cannot say 'must hold.'

x-m-m1-04.title: Fixing a sign judgment as information grows
x-m-m1-04.goal: Receive information about the signs of a product and a sum of integers one piece at a time, say only what is certain, and finally build an example that satisfies the conditions.
x-m-m1-04.material: We will give you information about the integers a and b one piece at a time. Each time the information grows, choose only what you can say for certain. (For example, you may try suitable numbers and think about which cases are possible.)
x-m-m1-04.thinking.0: Telling what is certain from what is not
x-m-m1-04.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment with new information
x-m-m1-04.thinking.2: Making an example that satisfies all the conditions
x-m-m1-04.prereq.0: Sign rules for adding and multiplying integers
x-m-m1-04.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of negative and positive numbers
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.prompt: Read the information one step at a time, and choose what you can say for certain from the information so far.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, try to make an example of numbers for which it could be wrong.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check that the information from earlier steps does not conflict with this choice.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say for certain from this information alone?
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If the product is negative, neither number is 0 and the two numbers have different signs. We do not yet know which one is positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: a=−2, b=3 also gives a negative product. The sign of a is not yet decided.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The two numbers have different signs
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You looked at the cases in which the product is negative.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: At least one of the two numbers is 0
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If one is 0, the product is 0. That conflicts with the information that the product is negative.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: If a=−2, b=5, the product is negative but the sum is positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What can you say for certain now?
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If the signs are different and the sum is positive, the positive one is farther from 0. We still do not know which one is positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The absolute value of the positive number is greater than the absolute value of the negative number
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You worked out which one has to be farther from 0 for the sum to be positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The absolute value of the negative number is greater
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If the negative one is farther from 0, the sum is negative.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The two numbers have the same absolute value
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If the absolute values are the same and the signs are different, the sum is 0.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: From Information 2 alone, we cannot tell which of a and b is positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What are the signs of a and b?
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If the signs are different and a<b, then a is negative and b is positive. Combining this with Information 2, we can also tell that |a|<|b|.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: a is positive, b is negative
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If a<b, then a is smaller. A positive number cannot be smaller than a negative number.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Information 1 said the signs are different.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: a is negative, b is positive
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You overlapped all three pieces of information and narrowed the possible cases down to one.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: We still cannot decide the signs
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Looking at a<b together with 'the signs are different' settles it.
x-m-m1-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, only 'the signs are different' was certain, but each new piece of information reduced the possible cases, and in the end it was settled that a<0<b. At the point where your judgment changed, tell which new information changed it.
x-m-m1-04.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different integer pairs (a, b) that satisfy all three pieces of information.
x-m-m1-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the signs of a and b, then adjust their sizes so that the sum is positive.
x-m-m1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute the numbers you found into the three conditions one at a time to check.
x-m-m1-04.s.s2.fail.c4: a is not less than b.
x-m-m1-04.s.s2.explain: The answer is every integer pair where a is negative, b is positive, and |a|<|b|. Examples: (−2, 5), (−1, 3), (−4, 9).

x-m-m1-05.title: Picking out the expressions that describe the matchstick pattern
x-m-m1-05.goal: Compare several expressions for a pattern, choose with reasons which expressions are always correct, and explain why an expression that works for only one or two values is risky.
x-m-m1-05.thinking.2: Telling apart cases that work by chance
x-m-m1-05.prereq.0: The meaning of expressions that use letters
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions that always correctly give the number of matchsticks for n squares.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute n=1 into each expression and compare with 4, the value for 1 square.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.hint.1: For expressions that were right at n=1, also check n=2 and n=3. Do not decide from a single value.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.r.a: Check whether you left out parentheses when putting 4 for each square and subtracting the (n−1) overlaps. Check whether the value is 4 when n=1.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.r.b: You substituted n=1, 2, 3 and checked that 4, 7, 10 came out, so you have solid reasons.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.r.c: You read it with the rule that the first square takes 4 and each additional square adds 3.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.r.d: It happens to be right at n=2 with 7, but did you also check n=1 or n=3?
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.r.e: You read it as an expression that counts the 2n horizontal sides and the (n+1) vertical sides separately.
x-m-m1-05.s.s1.explain: For b, c, and e, the values at n=1, 2, 3 are 4, 7, 10, and they all simplify to 3n+1. Expression a simplifies to 3n−1, so it gives 2 at n=1. Expression d happens to give 7 only at n=2, and gives 3 at n=1 and 11 at n=3, so it is not correct.
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.prompt: Show why one of the expressions you did not choose is wrong. Write what number you substituted for n and what you compared the value with.
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one expression and pick one number to substitute for n.
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find where the 'actual number of matchsticks' to compare with the value of the expression was given.
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: For the n you chose, did the value of the expression and the actual count really differ?
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write it knowing that an expression that is right for only one value can still be wrong?
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.model.0: Substituting n=1 into 4n−n−1 gives 4−1−1=2, but 1 square actually needs 4 matchsticks, so they differ. That is why it is wrong.
x-m-m1-05.s.s2.model.1: 4n−1 is right at n=2 with 7, but at n=1 it gives 3 while the actual number is 4, so it is wrong. An expression is not correct just because it is right for one value.

x-m-m1-06.title: Choosing the information that is really needed in an age problem
x-m-m1-06.goal: In an age problem, tell apart the information that is really needed to fix the daughter's age from information that is useless or repeats what we know, and then choose a sum yourself.
x-m-m1-06.material: A mother is 28 years older than her daughter. The daughter's age is a natural number. This information alone cannot fix the daughter's age to a single value. If one more piece of information from below is given, which one alone can fix the daughter's age to a single value?
x-m-m1-06.thinking.1: Telling new information from what we already knew
x-m-m1-06.thinking.2: Making values that satisfy the conditions
x-m-m1-06.prereq.0: Using a letter to stand for an unknown number
x-m-m1-06.prereq.1: The meaning of equalities and equations
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information that, given as just one more piece, can fix the daughter's age to a single value.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.hint.0: Let the daughter's age be x and write the mother's age in terms of x.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.hint.1: When you turn each piece of information into an equation and it matches an equation you already have, it is not new information.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.o.a: 10 years ago, the mother was also 28 years older than the daughter
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.r.a: '10 years ago' appears, so it looks new, but the age difference is always the same. It is a fact we already know.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.o.b: The sum of their current ages is 52
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.r.b: You considered whether it gives a new relationship linking the two ages, other than the age difference.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.o.c: The daughter is 28 years younger than the mother
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.r.c: It only says the 'mother is 28 years older' the other way around.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.o.d: The mother is taller than the daughter
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.r.d: This information has nothing to do with age. You cannot fix the age with numbers.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.o.e: The mother's current age is 3 times the daughter's age
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.r.e: It gives a new relationship between the daughter's age and the mother's age.
x-m-m1-06.s.s1.explain: If the daughter's age is x, the mother is x+28. Option b makes the new equation x+(x+28)=52 and option e makes x+28=3x, and x is fixed to one value (12 and 14 years old, respectively). Options a and c just restate something we already know, and d has nothing to do with age.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.prompt: Let's make a problem by choosing the sum of the two ages as S years. Make 3 different pairs (x, S) where the daughter's age x comes out exactly as a natural number and the sum S is less than 100.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the daughter's age first, find the mother's age, and then calculate the sum.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.hint.1: If you choose the sum S first, check whether the daughter's age comes out as a natural number.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.var.S: The sum S of the two ages
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The daughter's age is a natural number.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The daughter's age must be a natural number that is at least 1.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the two ages is S.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Adding the daughter's age x and the mother's age x+28 does not give S.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.explain: S=2x+28, so the daughter's age is a natural number only when S is an even number greater than 28. Examples: (12, 52), (5, 38), (30, 88).
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why S should not be chosen as 51 years.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the equation for x when S=51.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether the x that satisfies that equation is a natural number.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation show what x turns out to be when S=51?
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does the same problem happen with other odd values of S?
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.model.0: If S=51, then 2x+28=51, so x is 11.5, which is not a natural number.
x-m-m1-06.s.s2.because.model.1: The sum cannot be odd. 28 is even, so for the sum to work, x+x must also be even.

x-m-m1-07.title: Fixing the wrong line in an equation solution
x-m-m1-07.goal: Find the wrong line in the solution of a linear equation, reveal the error by substituting the solution back into the original equation, and correct it.
x-m-m1-07.material: Harin solved the linear equation 5x − 4 = 2x + 8 as shown below.
x-m-m1-07.thinking.0: Finding where the error is in the solution
x-m-m1-07.thinking.1: Checking the solution by substituting it back
x-m-m1-07.prereq.1: The meaning of terms and coefficients
x-m-m1-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Harin's solution.
x-m-m1-07.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute x=4/3 into both sides of the very first equation, and check whether the two values are equal.
x-m-m1-07.s.s1.hint.1: If the two sides are different, find the line where the equation first changed in the solution.
x-m-m1-07.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. When −4 is moved to the right side, its sign changes and it should become +4, but it was left as −4. Lines 3 and 4 follow from line 2, so their calculations are correct, but the result is wrong.
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.prompt: Write what happens when you substitute x=4/3 into the original equation, and write the corrected solution.
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate the value of each side as a fraction.
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute your corrected solution back into the original equation and check that both sides are equal.
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate and find that the two sides really have different values when x=4/3?
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you substitute your corrected solution into the original equation?
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.model.0: Substituting 4/3 gives 8/3 on the left and 32/3 on the right, which are different, so it is not the solution. Moving −4 over makes it +4, so 3x=12, x=4.
x-m-m1-07.s.s2.model.1: Checking with x=4 gives 16 on the left and 16 on the right, which are equal. Moving −4 to the right side changes its sign to +4, so 3x=12.

x-m-m1-08.title: Reading a water-height graph made of points
x-m-m1-08.goal: As points are added one by one, guess the pattern, fix your prediction when new points appear, and think about whether you can be sure of values between points.
x-m-m1-08.material: We measured the height of water while pouring water into a tank. The horizontal axis is time (minutes) and the vertical axis is height (cm). We write (time, height) as an ordered pair and plot it as a point on the coordinate plane. Several points are revealed at a time.
x-m-m1-08.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment with new data
x-m-m1-08.thinking.2: Judging values in an interval that was not measured
x-m-m1-08.prereq.0: Showing ordered pairs as points on the coordinate plane
x-m-m1-08.prereq.1: Reading what the horizontal and vertical axes mean
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.prompt: Answer the question each time points are revealed. It is fine if your earlier prediction changes.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare how much the height of the points changes each time the time increases by 1 minute.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the new point matches your earlier prediction, and if it does not, think about what story you should come up with.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What would you predict the height to be at 3 minutes?
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.after: The three points follow the same rule (4 cm per minute), so 12 cm at 3 minutes is natural. But it is not certain until the next point appears.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This does not continue the increase of the first 2 minutes.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You continued the rule of rising 4 cm every minute.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We do not know yet. We need more points
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You took into account that there are few points. That is reasonable, but you can already make an estimate from the points given now.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You assumed that the height suddenly rises faster than at the start. Check whether there is evidence for that.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: What would you predict the height to be at 6 minutes?
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.after: So far, predicting 24 cm is natural, but since we do not know the height of the tank, you can also think about the case where it is full (20 cm).
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Check whether you have a reason to think it slows down from the speed it was rising at.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You kept going with the rule of rising 4 cm per minute.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought of the possibility that the tank is full.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Check whether you have a reason to think the rising speed suddenly gets faster.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which explanation is possible for what happened from minute 6 to minute 8?
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The fact that the three points have the same height alone cannot fix a single reason. We need other information (the height of the tank, whether water is still being supplied).
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The water height keeps rising, but the ruler showed the same value
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It is hard to blame only the ruler for getting the same value three times in a row.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The tank is full, so it cannot rise any more
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You looked to the tank for the reason the height cannot rise further.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The pouring of water was stopped
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought of the simplest reason the height does not change.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Water drains out at the same rate as it is poured in
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You thought that if the amount coming in and going out is the same, the height does not change.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.after: At some point after minute 8, water begins to drain and the height drops 4 cm every minute. The reason the earlier prediction (24 cm) was wrong also connects to this story.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.o.a: Water is draining out and the height is going down
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You read the change of dropping 4 cm every minute.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.r.b: The height went from 20 to 16 to 12. Read it again.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.o.c: The tank overflowed, so the height dropped
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.r.c: If it overflows, the height stops at the height of the tank. It does not drop.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.o.d: There are only two points, so we cannot say anything
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Even with just two points, you can confirm that the height decreased.
x-m-m1-08.s.s1.reflect: Each time points were added, the prediction and the explanation changed. At first we continued the rule, but after minute 6 the points broke the rule. Tell where it was hard to fix a single explanation by looking only at the points.
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.prompt: If you join the points (8, 20) and (9, 16) with a line segment, you can read the height at 8.5 minutes as 18 cm. Can we trust this value? Write your reason.
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.hint.0: Look at how many points there are between minute 8 and minute 9.
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think of two stories about how the water height could have moved in between.
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the value from the line segment is a 'guessed value,' not a 'measured value'?
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give at least one other case that could have happened in between?
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.model.0: We did not measure between minute 8 and minute 9, so we cannot know whether it is 18 cm at 8.5 minutes. It might have stayed at 20 cm until 8 minutes 30 seconds and then suddenly dropped.
x-m-m1-08.s.s2.model.1: There are only two points and no measured values in between, so we cannot be sure it is 18 cm. We could check by measuring at shorter intervals than 1 minute.

x-m-m1-09.title: Finding triangle sticks with perimeter 15
x-m-m1-09.goal: Test what relationship three stick lengths must have to make a triangle, find several sets of three lengths that fit the conditions, and explain why some do not work.
x-m-m1-09.material: We want to make a triangle by joining three sticks, whose lengths are natural numbers (cm), end to end. The sticks cannot be bent or stretched. The three lengths add up to 15 cm, and all three lengths are different. (Picture description: put the longest stick on the floor, then stand the other two sticks up from its two ends so that they meet at the top.)
x-m-m1-09.thinking.0: Reasoning out the condition for making a triangle
x-m-m1-09.thinking.2: Explaining why impossible cases are impossible
x-m-m1-09.prereq.0: The meaning of the sides and perimeter of a triangle
x-m-m1-09.prereq.1: Your experience drawing triangles with an unmarked ruler and a compass
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.prompt: We want to find out whether the three sticks 3 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm can make a triangle. What is the best first thing to do?
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine that you put the longest stick, 8 cm, on the floor.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare 8 cm with the length of the other two sticks joined in a line.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.o.a: First work out whether the sum of the three lengths is even or odd
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.r.a: Whether the sum is even or odd has nothing to do with whether a triangle can be made.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.o.b: Assume that it is always possible if the three lengths are different, and draw it right away
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.r.b: The fact that the lengths are different alone does not tell you whether they connect. Test it with 3, 4, 8.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.o.c: Join the sticks in order starting from the shortest and see whether it closes
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.r.c: No matter which stick you put down first, it is the same figure. The order of joining is not the key point.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.o.d: Put the longest stick on the floor and work out whether the ends of the other two sticks touch
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.r.d: You focused on whether the two sticks standing up from the two ends can meet.
x-m-m1-09.s.s1.explain: If you put the longest stick on the floor, the ends of the other two sticks cannot touch when their joined length is shorter than the floor stick. 3+4=7<8, so 3, 4, 8 cannot make a triangle.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different sets of three sides (a, b, c) of a triangle with perimeter 15 cm and all three lengths different. Sets that only change the order are the same triangle.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the range of lengths that the longest side could be.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a candidate, then compare the longest side with the sum of the other two sides.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The three lengths are natural numbers.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The three lengths must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three lengths is not 15.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.fail.c4: A triangle cannot be made with these lengths.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.explain: Only three are possible: (2, 6, 7), (3, 5, 7), (4, 5, 6). In every one, the longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two sides.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.prompt: (1, 5, 9) has perimeter 15 but cannot make a triangle. Write the reason.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the longest stick, 9, on the floor and try standing the other two sticks up.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the length of the other two sticks joined in a line with 9.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the longest side with the other two sides?
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does the same reason work for other lengths (for example, 2, 4, 9)?
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The longest side, 9, is longer than the sum of the other two sides, 1+5=6, so the ends of the two sticks do not meet.
x-m-m1-09.s.s2.because.model.1: No matter how far apart you spread 1 and 5, they cannot reach 9. The long side 9 is longer than 6, the sum of the two short sides, so it does not work.

x-m-m1-10.title: Does a bigger frequency mean they did better?
x-m-m1-10.goal: Learn the problem with comparing frequencies as they are when two classes have different numbers of students, and tell apart what the table lets you say for certain from what it does not.
x-m-m1-10.material:
Class 1 (20 students) and Class 2 (50 students) took the same math test. The frequency distribution table with scores grouped into three intervals is as follows.
Interval / Class 1 (20 students) / Class 2 (50 students)
Below 60 points / 2 students / 10 students
60 points or more but below 80 points / 10 students / 25 students
80 points or more / 8 students / 15 students
Minji said, "There are more students with 80 points or more in Class 2, with 15, so Class 2 did better on the test."
x-m-m1-10.thinking.0: Judging the evidence for a claim
x-m-m1-10.thinking.1: Telling what the table does and does not show
x-m-m1-10.thinking.2: Arguing against a claim with numbers
x-m-m1-10.prereq.0: How to read a frequency distribution table
x-m-m1-10.prereq.1: The meaning of frequency and the total number of students
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the things you can say for certain from the table alone.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each class, divide the number of students in that interval by the total number of students in that class.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether any choice uses information that is not in the table (such as the mean) in its conclusion.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.o.a: The proportion of students with below 60 points in Class 2 is 2 times that in Class 1
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.r.a: You divided by the total number of students in each class and compared the proportions.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.o.b: The mean score of Class 2 is higher than that of Class 1
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.r.b: In a table with grouped intervals, you cannot know the mean exactly, because you do not know the scores inside each interval.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.o.c: There are more students with 80 points or more in Class 2, so Class 2 did better on the test
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.r.c: You compared two classes with different numbers of students using only the number of students. Look again in terms of the total number of students.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.o.d: The proportion of students with 80 points or more is higher in Class 1 than in Class 2
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.r.d: You divided by the total number of students in each class and compared the proportions.
x-m-m1-10.s.s1.explain: In terms of proportions, for 80 points or more, Class 1 has 8/20=40% and Class 2 has 15/50=30%, so Class 1 is higher; for below 60 points, Class 1 has 2/20=10% and Class 2 has 10/50=20%, so Class 2 is 2 times Class 1. The mean cannot be known from a table with grouped intervals, and a conclusion that compares only the number of students has weak support.
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply that argues against Minji's statement. Use numbers to explain why you should not compare only the number of students.
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of students with 80 points or more and the total number of students for each class side by side.
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think about a way to compare the two classes on the same basis.
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do the numbers you wrote match the numbers in the table?
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you show that Minji's conclusion could be reversed?
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.model.0: The classes have different numbers of students, so we should not compare using only the number of students. For 80 points or more, Class 1 has 8÷20=40% and Class 2 has 15÷50=30%, so Class 1 is higher.
x-m-m1-10.s.s2.model.1: Class 1 has 8 out of 20 students in total, and Class 2 has 15 out of 50 students in total. In terms of relative frequency, they are 0.4 and 0.3, so Class 1 is actually higher.
